title: Time terms reversed temperature gains for warm-year Meadow Brown date predictions in two English regions in 2002-2024
abstract: We tested Meadow Brown mean flight-date predictions in the five warmest springs in two English regions and two periods. Site and time models with and without spring temperature used fixed site sets with at least 80 percent record coverage. Temperature gains were +8.60 and +17.33 days squared in southern and northern England in 1980-2001, but -4.52 and -13.64 in 2002-2024. Positive gain means less error with temperature. Removing time terms made later gains positive in both regions. Removing one test year could also reverse both later gain signs. Warm-year errors were not consistently above the median of 500 random five-year holdouts. These are observed score contrasts, not population effects. Random ranges and year-deletion ranges are not confidence intervals. Small samples, missing visits, coarse weather and correlated regional weather limit inference. The test does not identify a causal climate effect or a daily heat-extreme effect. The package gives code, source hashes, aggregate evidence and reproduction instructions. External databases remain outside the signed package.

display.caption: Prediction errors and temperature gains for five warmest spring years, compared with random five-year holdouts. Random 5–95 percent ranges are reference ranges, not confidence intervals. Contains UKBMS data; full source attribution is in the text and external data notice.

citations.reason: Prior chronological model transfer in the same archive. We add warm-temperature blocks within two periods, rather than later chronological holdouts. Observations overlap.
Prior regional Meadow Brown temperature slopes motivate testing prediction rather than fitted slope signs.
Prior climate and ozone support audit compared later and random splits for US birds. This study instead scores biological predictions in warm-year blocks.
